module_title: Computer Generations - Programming Languages, Memory Storage, and Milestone Machines
introduction: This intermediate tier deep-dives into how software and memory evolved alongside hardware. We explore the transition of programming languages, the shift from punch cards to magnetic storage, and the crucial 'Stored Program Concept' that defined modern architecture.

core_concepts.title: Evolution of Programming Languages
core_concepts.description: 1st Gen: Exclusively used 'Machine Language' (Binary 0s and 1s). 2nd Gen: Saw the introduction of 'Assembly Language' and early high-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL. 3rd Gen: Widespread use of 'High-Level Languages' (PASCAL, BASIC, C).

core_concepts.title: Evolution of Memory & Storage
core_concepts.description: 1st Gen: Relied on 'Magnetic Drums' for memory and Punch Cards for input. 2nd & 3rd Gen: Shifted to 'Magnetic Core' memory for primary storage, and magnetic tapes/disks for secondary storage.

core_concepts.title: The Stored Program Concept
core_concepts.description: Introduced by 'John von Neumann', this concept proposed that both data and programming instructions should be stored in the same memory unit. The EDVAC (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer) was one of the first machines to utilize this architecture.

core_concepts.title: UNIVAC
core_concepts.description: Stands for 'Universal Automatic Computer'. It holds the record as the world's first commercially successful electronic digital computer, famously used to predict the 1952 US Presidential election.

important_entities.name: Ada Lovelace
important_entities.significance: She wrote the first algorithm intended to be processed by Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

important_entities.name: Jack Kilby & Robert Noyce
important_entities.significance: They independently co-invented the IC in 1958, miniaturizing electronic circuits onto a single piece of semiconductor material.

important_entities.name: Douglas Engelbart
important_entities.significance: He invented the first computer mouse (made of wood) in the 1960s, revolutionizing Human-Computer Interaction (HCI).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The First Electronic Computer Debate (ENIAC vs. ABC)
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: While ENIAC is widely known, if an exam asks for the 'First Automatic Electronic Digital Computer' and 'ABC' (Atanasoff-Berry Computer) is in the options, select ABC. It predated ENIAC but was not general-purpose (it was built to solve linear equations).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The Material of an IC Chip
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very common static GK question: 'What is an IC chip made of?' The answer is always 'Silicon' (or sometimes Germanium), which is a Semiconductor.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: 1st Gen: M (Machine Language) -> 2nd Gen: A (Assembly Language) -> 3rd Gen: H (High-Level Language).

exam_strategy_tips: Examiners frequently test the Full Forms of early legacy computers. Ensure you have memorized ENIAC, EDVAC, and UNIVAC thoroughly for banking and SSC mains.
